ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: As shown in the figure, the primary and secondary coils of an ideal transformer are respectively connected to bulbs a and b with the same rated voltage. When the input voltage U is 10 times the rated voltage of the bulbs, both bulbs can emit light normally. What is the ratio of turns of the primary coil to the secondary coil?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, the primary and secondary coils of an ideal transformer are respectively connected to bulbs a and b with the same rated voltage. When the input voltage U is 10 times the rated voltage of the bulbs, both bulbs can emit light normally. What is the ratio of turns of the primary coil to the secondary coil?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, the left side is the circuit where the primary coil of the transformer is located, and the externally applied input voltage is marked as U; bulb a is drawn on the upper wire on the left side, and is in the same series circuit as the primary coil. The right side is the secondary coil circuit, and bulb b is connected in the closed circuit formed by the two ends of the secondary coil. Then reason: let the common rated voltage of bulbs a and b be V. The problem says both bulbs emit light normally, so the voltage across bulb a is V, and the voltage across bulb b is also V. Also, the input voltage U is 10 times the rated voltage of the bulbs, namely U=10V. Since in the figure bulb a is in series with the primary coil, the voltage across the primary coil is 10V−V=9V. The secondary coil supplies power to bulb b, and the voltage across the secondary coil is V. An ideal transformer satisfies that the turns ratio equals the voltage ratio of the corresponding coils, therefore N1:N2=U1:U2=9V:V=9:1.
